en: The Apadāna of the Elder Gandhodakiya From the Bījanī Chapter, the Fourth I was a merchant in the city of Rājagaha, and I was known as the perfumer. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, had arrived at Rājagaha. Having heard that the Teacher had come, I went to the Jetavana grove to see the Blessed One. There, I saw the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, seated amidst a circle of monks, like the moon surrounded by the stars. Having seen the Teacher, I paid homage with my head at his feet and sat down to one side. As I sat there, the Blessed One, out of compassion for me, preached the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, I attained the fruit of stream-entry. Then, having taken leave of the Blessed One, I returned to my own home. I prepared a vessel filled with scented water and offered it to the Blessed One. Having made this offering, I spoke these words: "May I, through this root of merit, become a Perfume-Scattering Buddha in the future. By virtue of that deed, I have now been reborn in the world of the Thirty-three gods. Here, I am known as Gandhodakiya, and I dwell in the midst of the gods. Because of that gift of scented water, I enjoy great splendor and glory. When the Blessed One passed away, he entered the realm of Nibbāna. Then, the King of Kings, Ajātasattu, caused a stūpa to be built for the Tathāgata. When the stūpa was completed, I took a handful of flowers and scattered them over the stūpa of the Great Sage. By that deed, I have now attained the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, having performed various deeds in the past, I have now attained the fruit of stream-entry. May all beings be well and happy. May they live long and free from disease. May all their wishes be fulfilled. May they attain the bliss of Nibbāna. May the world be prosperous and peaceful. May all beings be happy. “During the time of Padumuttara Buddha,
there was a great festival for the Bodhi tree;
[I] took a variegated water-pot, and...”
I offered scented water.
And at the time of the Bodhi tree’s bathing,
a great cloud rained down.
And there was a great roar as the thunderbolt crashed;
by that very force of the lightning strike,
Having passed away there,
while dwelling in the world of the gods,
I spoke these verses.
“Oh, the Buddhas! Oh, the Dhamma!
Oh, our accomplishment of a Teacher!
My physical body has fallen away.”
I delight in the world of the gods.
My celestial palace is lofty,
with a hundred stories, rising high into the sky.
Hundreds of thousands of maidens always attend upon me;
no ailments exist for me.
Sorrow does not exist for me;
I see no feverish distress—
this is the fruit of meritorious deeds.
In the twenty-eighth century of eons,
I was King Saṃvasita,
endowed with the seven treasures.
A wheel-turning monarch of great power.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth]...
“Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
Thus indeed did the venerable elder Gandhodakiya recite these verses.
This is the fourth legend of the elder Gandhodakiya.
